platforms.title: 3 Foods That Quietly Raise Your Gout Risk
platforms.meta_description: A big toe that suddenly turns red, swollen, and painful to the touch isn't random. Three foods and drinks raise uric acid enough to trigger a gout attack.
platforms.body_html:
A big toe or knee that suddenly turns red, swollen, and painful enough that even a bedsheet touching it hurts is the classic sign of a gout attack. It isn't random — three specific foods and drinks measurably raise the uric acid that causes it.

Why It Lands in the Big Toe Specifically

Purines are compounds found naturally in many foods and in the body's own cells. When the body breaks purines down, uric acid is the byproduct, and normally the kidneys filter most of it out through urine. In gout, the kidneys can't clear enough uric acid, even when kidney function is otherwise normal, so it builds up in the blood and eventually forms sharp monosodium urate crystals. According to the National Kidney Foundation, those crystals settle more readily in cooler parts of the body, which is why the big toe — the joint farthest from the heart and the coolest in the body — is the most common site for a gout attack.

Oily fish like mackerel is one of the biggest dietary contributors — some cuts pack well over 150 milligrams of purine per 100 grams, among the highest of any commonly eaten food. Beer carries a double burden: it's high in purines from the yeast used to brew it, and separately, the lactic acid produced as the body metabolizes alcohol interferes with the kidneys' ability to excrete uric acid, according to the Merck Manual. Red meat, including seasoned short ribs and other marinated cuts, sits at a similar purine level to oily fish, so eating it often keeps uric acid persistently elevated rather than letting it settle back down between meals.

What Actually Lowers Your Risk

  • Swap oily fish for white fish like cod or flounder where you can, or at least cut your usual portion in half if giving it up isn't realistic.
  • Replace beer with non-alcoholic beer or sparkling water, and if you do drink it, match every serving with an equal amount of water to help support kidney clearance.
  • Swap red meat for tofu or eggs on more nights, and when you do eat meat, stick to lean cuts and smaller portions rather than large, marinated servings.
  • Drink more than 2 liters of water a day — staying well hydrated is one of the simplest, most consistently recommended habits for supporting the kidneys' ability to clear uric acid.

The CDC estimates gout affects close to 4 to 5 percent of adults in the United States, and it shows up in men roughly twice as often as in women, typically in their 40s and 50s, though attacks in women become more common after menopause. According to the National Kidney Foundation, left untreated over time, gout carries real downstream risk: kidney stones and kidney damage develop in an estimated 10 to 18 percent of people with the condition, alongside firm uric acid deposits called tophi that can form under the skin near affected joints.

None of this requires giving up fish, beer, or meat entirely — the goal is shifting the balance so uric acid has room to come back down between meals instead of staying elevated. If a joint flares up suddenly and stays swollen for more than a few days, or if attacks start happening more than once a year, that's worth bringing to a doctor, since long-term uncontrolled gout can damage joints and kidneys even between visible attacks.
